version: teaching spec v1.4 (Socrates), science spec v1 section 7 + tesla_answers_v1 (Tesla)
noDot: Not on this H-R diagram. A neutron star is far too small and faint for this chart, and a black hole has no surface to measure.
credit1Sun: 1 Sun track adjusted slightly so today's Sun matches measured values.

hub.caption: Pick a starting mass in Suns. It is your only choice: the mass sets the whole life, and the model plays it out.
What will your star become in the end?

act.q: What will your star become in the end?

hub.caption: Predict before you watch: place three guess pins on the H-R diagram for where it spends most of its life, where it swells the most, and where it ends. Then the model shows where it really goes.

formation.title: Cold cloud
formation.caption: A cloud of gas and dust, only 10 to 20 K. It glows in infrared and radio waves, but looks dark to your eyes.

formation.title: Collapse
formation.caption: Gravity pulls a dense core of the cloud inward. This free fall takes about 100,000 years.

formation.title: Protostar, disk and jets
formation.caption: A protostar forms in a spinning disk, with jets along its axis. It glows from squeezing under gravity, not from fusion.

captionBy.0.2: The young star is bigger and brighter than it will be on the main sequence. It shrinks over millions of years. A small star takes hundreds of millions of years to settle.
captionBy.1: The young star is bigger and brighter than it will be on the main sequence. It shrinks over millions of years. This young star (a T Tauri star) is no longer a protostar. The Sun took about 30 to 50 million years to get here. Planets form in the disk at the same time.
captionBy.3: A heavier star contracts faster, in about 3 million years.
captionBy.15: A heavy star contracts in well under 1 million years, still wrapped in its cloud. Its strong light soon blows its disk away.
captionBy.40: A heavy star contracts in well under 1 million years, still wrapped in its cloud. Its strong light soon blows its disk away.

1.q: When do the planets form: before the star, at the same time, or after it is done?

formation.title: Ignition
formation.caption: The core reaches about 10 million K and hydrogen fusion takes over. It is a gradual handover, not a flash.
chips: Stars fuse. They do not burn.

0.2.title: Red dwarf main sequence
0.2.caption: A red dwarf shines dimly, so it uses its fuel slowly. It also stirs its whole inside, so it can use nearly all its hydrogen. It lasts about 1 trillion years or more. The universe is 13.8 billion years old, so no red dwarf has ever died.

act.q: Will it live shorter than, about the same as, or longer than the Sun?

0.2.title: Late life (predicted)
0.2.caption: Predicted: late in life, models say it gets hotter and a little brighter, then shrinks into a helium white dwarf. Nobody has seen this.

0.2.title: Helium white dwarf (predicted)
0.2.caption: Predicted: it ends as a helium white dwarf, about Earth-size. It will cool forever.

1.title: Main sequence
1.caption: In space, the Sun looks white. It spends about 10 billion years near this spot on the diagram, and its dot only creeps.

act.q: What color is the Sun in space?
As the Sun ages, does its dot slide along the main sequence?
choices: no, it stays near one spot
act.answer: no, it stays near one spot

notes: On its own, the Sun is too light to explode or become a black hole. It will become a white dwarf.
In about 1 to 1.5 billion years from now, the brightening Sun will likely boil away Earth's oceans.

1.title: Subgiant and red giant
1.caption: The Sun swells to about 170 times its radius. Its surface cools to about 3,100 K, so it looks orange-red, yet it is about 2,300 times brighter. Later it swells even more. Earth may be swallowed. Astronomers aren't sure yet.

act.q: Red giant: hotter or cooler than the Sun? Brighter or dimmer?

1.title: Helium flash
1.caption: Helium ignites suddenly in a very dense core. It lasts minutes to hours and you cannot see it from outside.

1.title: Core helium fusion
1.caption: For about 100 million years, helium fuses to carbon in the core, with hydrogen fusing in a shell around it.

1.title: Asymptotic giant branch
1.caption: A second swelling, with strong winds. The Sun loses about half its mass before it becomes a white dwarf. Stars like this make some elements heavier than iron.

act.q: Predict: drag the mass meter to where you think the Sun will end.

1.title: Planetary nebula
1.caption: The star's outer layers drift away at about 10 to 30 km/s, lit by a hot core of 100,000 K or more. The name is a historical accident: in small telescopes these shells looked round like planets.

1.title: White dwarf
1.caption: A white dwarf is about Earth-size, with about half the Sun's mass. It shines from stored heat, not fusion, and slowly cools. No black dwarfs exist yet: cooling takes far longer than the age of the universe.

3.title: Main sequence
3.caption: A 3 Sun star is blue-white and about 80 times as bright as the Sun at first, and brighter later. It lasts about 300 to 400 million years.

act.q: How many times shorter is its life than the Sun's? About 3, 30, or 300?

3.title: Hertzsprung gap
3.caption: When hydrogen runs out in the core, it cools and grows fast, in a few million years.

act.q: Predict: when the hydrogen in its core runs out, which way will its dot move?

3.title: Red giant, quiet helium ignition
3.caption: As a red giant, it ignites helium quietly, with no flash.

3.title: Core helium fusion
3.caption: For tens of millions of years, helium fuses in the core.

3.title: Asymptotic giant branch
3.caption: A second swelling with strong winds, lasting several million years.

act.q: Predict: drag the mass meter to where you think the white dwarf will end up.

3.title: Planetary nebula and white dwarf
3.caption: Planetary nebula, then a carbon-oxygen white dwarf of about 0.7 Suns.

15.title: Main sequence
15.caption: A 15 Sun star is about 20,000 times as bright as the Sun. It lasts only about 13 million years.

act.q: Does a bigger star live longer or shorter than the Sun?

15.title: Red supergiant
15.caption: It swells to about 800 to 1,000 times the Sun's radius, cooling to about 3,300 to 3,500 K, and shines at about 75,000 to 100,000 Suns.

15.title: Fusion in shells
15.caption: Each fuel lasts shorter than the last. Silicon fusion lasts only about 18 days. Outside, the star barely changes.

act.q: How long does the last fuel, silicon, last?

15.title: Core collapse
15.caption: The core runs out of fuel that releases energy and collapses, in under 1 second.

choices: Iron fusion soaks up energy and makes it explode
The core runs out of fuel that releases energy
act.answer: The core runs out of fuel that releases energy

15.title: Supernova
15.caption: This kind of supernova happens when a massive star's core collapses. Debris moves at about 10,000 km/s. It can rival a whole galaxy for weeks, but about 99 percent of its energy leaves as neutrinos.
chips: Supernovae make many elements and scatter them into space, including some heavier than iron.

15.title: Neutron star
15.caption: At 15 Suns, a neutron star is the most likely result: about 1.4 Suns in a ball about 12 km in radius.
chips: Neutron star mergers also make elements heavier than iron, such as gold.

40.title: Main sequence
40.caption: A 40 Sun star is blue-white at about 40,000 to 45,000 K and about 200,000 to 300,000 times as bright as the Sun. It lasts only about 5 million years.

act.q: Will it swell into a red supergiant like the 15 Sun star?
act.reveal: The model swells it to a yellow supergiant by 4.99 million years. After that, models differ.

40.title: Strong winds
40.caption: Strong winds blow off a large part of its mass. It may never become a red supergiant, and may end as a hot Wolf-Rayet star.

act.q: Predict: drag the mass meter to where you think it ends.

40.title: Fusion in shells
40.caption: The same fuel stages as the 15 Sun star, but each one is faster.
40.bars: each fuel lasts shorter than the last
40.level2: For a 25 Sun star (Woosley, Heger and Weaver 2002): hydrogen 6.7 million years, helium 0.84 million years, carbon 520 years, neon 0.9 years, oxygen 0.4 years, silicon about 0.7 days.

40.title: Core collapse
40.caption: The core runs out of fuel that releases energy and collapses.

40.title: Two paths
40.caption: Scientists are not sure how stars this massive die. Some may explode first. Others may collapse with little or no visible explosion. A few candidates have been seen, such as N6946-BH1, but none is confirmed yet.
chips: Both paths at once: the faint shell is a possible explosion. The star itself fades in a quiet collapse.

40.title: Black hole
40.caption: Most stars this massive are expected to leave black holes, but some may leave neutron stars. Far from it, a black hole pulls like any object of the same mass.
labels: A black hole, probably 5 to 20 or more times the Sun's mass. Black holes from stars in our galaxy measured so far mostly fall in this range.
about 3 km of radius for each Sun of mass

act.q: A planet sits at the same distance from this black hole as it would from a star with the same mass. Is the pull stronger, the same, or weaker?
act.optionalReveal: This black hole has less mass than the star had, so from its old distance the pull is actually weaker.

pp.title: Proton-proton chain (the Sun)
lines: p + p -> deuterium + positron + neutrino (happens twice)
Net: 4 protons -> 1 helium-4 + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy (about 26.7 MeV)
The total number of protons plus neutrons stays at 4. Two protons turn into neutrons.

triple.title: Triple-alpha
lines: Then carbon-12 + helium-4 -> oxygen-16 + gamma ray.

nife.title: Nickel to iron
lines: Each step turns a proton into a neutron and gives off gamma rays. This decay powers the supernova's glow for months.
nife.extra: Another kind, Type Ia, involves a white dwarf in a binary. It is not shown here.
